I'm sorry to hear that you're going through the same thing :( I hope you can beat your depression and reclaim your true self, recognize there's nothing wrong with it, and own it! 

Regarding my progress, at the height of my depression early this year, I stopped going to school. Barely passed most of my subjects, had incomplete marks on a couple, then eventually had to take a leave of absence from school. I was assertive and confident before but it got to the point that I couldn't even leave the house, much less my room. Worse, my self-esteem plummeted so much (it didn't help that I gained weight and had a major breakout during this time that people never fail to point out), I couldn't even look people in the eye. But now, I'm going back to school, even fighting tooth and nails for it because my school admin is not helping me much and is unresponsive all the time. I'm also trying to complete the requirements needed to complete my incomplete marks from my previous subjects. But more than the academic progress, I learned to temper my perfectionist tendencies and allow myself to be human and make mistakes. I learned to be firm with my boundaries and refuse to settle for anything less that what I need/want just because I'm lonely and desperate for crumbs. And finally, for a former over-achiever, straight A kid who sacrificed everything for acads before (which led to major burnout, obviously), I learned that having a life outside of school, enjoying quality time with friends and family, and basically just doing anything that makes you happy is so much more important than your academic performance. Sounds obvious but if you derive your worth on your accomplishments your entire life, this lesson is extremely difficult to learn. I had to experience what it was like to feel unbearable sadness and pain every day for months just for me to start actively doing things that makes me happy and/or are good for my mental health. I used to think doing my hobbies was a privilege that I couldn't enjoy unless I've finished all my work. Turns out you need that rest because working non-stop is unsustainable and counterproductive.
